topic: Knowing your role and when to refer
sourceSummary: Page 6. Sets out the student's role, six steps for passing on a concern, and what must go to a supervisor straight away. The steps are a procedure learners will be observed doing in Task 3.

keyIdeas: Students on placement do not give medical information or counselling.
A concern is passed on in six steps, the same shift, in person.
Any mention of self-harm or risk to others goes to a supervisor immediately.
analysis.threshold: Passing something on is part of the job done well, not a failure to handle it.
analysis.skill: Pass on a concern in the right order, and know what cannot wait.

candidates.name: Passing on a concern, in order
candidates.angle: The six steps shuffled. Learners put them in order, and each misplaced step explains what goes wrong when it comes too early or too late. It rehearses the procedure Task 3 observes.
candidates.payoff: Pass on a concern in the right order.

sketch.title: Passing on a concern
sketch.intent: Learners can pass on a family member's concern in the order their service expects.
sketch.goal: pass on a family member's concern in the right order.
sketch.prompt: A family member tells you something that worries you. Put these steps in the order you would take them.

items.label: Listen without interrupting
items.why: You cannot pass on accurately what you did not hear in full.

items.label: Acknowledge what they have said
items.why: It tells them they were heard before anything else happens.

items.label: Tell them you will pass it on, and to whom
items.why: They should never be surprised that someone else knows.

items.label: Tell your supervisor the same shift, in person
items.why: A note alone can sit unread. In person, the same shift, it gets acted on.

items.label: Record it in the progress notes
items.why: The record comes after the conversation with your supervisor, as your service requires.

items.label: Check back with the family that someone has followed up
items.why: Closing the loop is what the family remembers, and it catches the follow-ups that did not happen.

sources.label: Course page: Knowing your role and when to refer
sources.note: The order of steps is from the page. The reasons were written for this activity.

candidates.name: What cannot wait?
candidates.angle: Before the steps, learners pick which of three things a family member might say must go to a supervisor immediately. The two that can wait make the one that cannot stand out.
candidates.payoff: Recognise a concern that must be referred straight away.

sketch.title: What cannot wait?
sketch.intent: Learners can recognise a concern that must go to their supervisor immediately.
sketch.goal: recognise a concern that must go to your supervisor straight away.
sketch.question: Three things a family member says to you on one shift. Which one goes to your supervisor straight away, not at the end of the shift?

options.label: "Mum's cardigan has gone missing from the laundry again."
options.feedback: Worth passing on, but it can wait for the end of the shift.

options.label: "Dad keeps saying he doesn't want to go on any more."
options.feedback: Right. Any mention of not wanting to go on goes to your supervisor immediately.

options.label: "When is the doctor next visiting?"
options.feedback: Find out or pass it on, but it is not urgent.

reveal.heading: Some things cannot wait
reveal.explanation: Any mention of self-harm, of not wanting to go on, or of a risk to someone else goes to your supervisor immediately, in person. Everything else still gets passed on, the same shift.
